documents.text:
[SPEAKER_00]
What's up? Welcome back to Seed to Harvest, a podcast focusing on stories and tactics from a diverse array of investors, founders, and creators, hosted by me, Paige Van Doherty. I'm the founding partner behind Genius Ventures and the author of an illustrated children's book about venture, also called Seed to Harvest.

[SPEAKER_01]
You can do venture differently. You don't have to follow anybody's path. When you want to do something that people think is crazy, you'll get a lot of naysayers. Just do it.

[SPEAKER_00]
I'm really excited to be here today with Matt Conwell, the founding partner of Rare Breed Ventures and an enthusiastic drag racer. Before we hop into today's episode, a quick word from our sponsor. If you're a startup founder, you know early decisions can be the difference between success and failure. One decision that thousands of successful founders have made is choosing Stripe as their payments platform. Fun fact, at Seed to Harvest, I used Stripe Atlas to incorporate my company. It was super easy and simple to incorporate my company, especially with their thorough instructions. I was able to set up a bank account and start accepting payments through Stripe. And over the past decade, Stripe has supported the growth of the most ambitious businesses, including Shopify, Lyft, and Kickstarter. Stripe uniquely knows how to support startups from their Atlas product that allows you to turn your idea into a business by helping you incorporate quickly, to their capital product that provides funding to help you scale your startup. Stripe has the tools you need to grow your business. And if you want to learn how Stripe can support you, visit Stripe.com today. That's Stripe.com to get started today. Now let's dive in. I'm really excited to share a bit of Mac's story, how he spends his time and how he makes investment decisions. So what is your North Star, Mac?

[SPEAKER_01]
So my North Star is this amazing black woman here in Baltimore. I watched this woman for three years try to convince people that her idea of a tumble dryer that can dry a wig or hair extension in 15 minutes with no heat was a valuable idea. I watched her get nothing but no's to the point where she determined that her only option in order to get access to capital to start building her first prototype was by becoming a surrogate mother. She gave birth to twins to raise a nominal amount of money just so she could start building a prototype. And to watch her go through that experience was truly frustrating for me, especially considering when you look at the wig and hair extension market, which is predicted to be a $10 billion market by the year 2023, with zero innovation in the care for the products, what she was building was like a true opportunity. And nobody else could see that.

[SPEAKER_00]
I think that's such an incredibly powerful story of what motivates you as an investor. So I believe that congratulations are in order as you have closed your first fund.

[SPEAKER_01]
Yes, we have closed fund one, a rare breed.

[SPEAKER_00]
All the flowers. I'm so happy for you, Mac. It's been such an incredible year, two years to be on this journey together. So I would love to hear more about like your experience fundraising, some of the fun and not so fun stories that came out of that.

[SPEAKER_01]
Fundraising is hard. You know, everybody talks about how hard it is. And then you start doing it and you realize it is like as hard, if not harder than what everybody says. Early on in the fundraising process, I recognized I didn't have a network of LPs. But I noticed that the more I tweeted about venture and entrepreneurship, the more other VCs will follow me. And so I just made it a point that if I saw there was a VC who followed me, I would send them a message to have a meeting. And so I had a lot of meetings in a short amount of time, but it did three things. One, it helped grow my profile and brand because now I had a larger group of people who knew me. Two, it helped me learn like how to fundraise and from other GPs and get advice. But then three, and the one that I wasn't expecting but was most important was a lot of these GPs, other funds started committing capital to my fund. And so like the first two to three million in my fund, which is a $10 million fund, all came from, the majority came from other GPs, other funds. And so like the Twitter thing became my strategy. And then also on top of that, AngelList last year came out, or in 2020, came out with their rolling funds. And, you know, those things started to get popular. One of the really interesting parts about rolling funds was they were able to publicly solicit. And so my Twitter presence is growing. I'm like, oh, the ability to publicly solicit would be a game changer for me. I got to do this. And really what it was is they were taking advantage of a designation that most funds hadn't, a 506C. The 506C designation actually comes from the Jobs Act from back in 2013, which allows for both funds and companies to raise capital in a public manner, but all their investors must be accredited. So for me, that gave me a clear option to talk about my fund publicly. And now I'm part of a wave that you, I would say, are part of as well, of these emerging funds that are doing what we call building in public, where we're keeping people involved and letting people know what we're doing at every step of the way in a very transparent way. It was allowing a lot of people to see how the industry works. And so I want to ask you, Paige, what's that been like for you, building in public? How's building in public been for you?

[SPEAKER_00]
Yeah, building in public's been super interesting. We've had a bit of divergent routes because we chose to raise under 506B, which means you can't solicit and you can't publicly talk about fundraising. So I honestly struggled with that. It was interesting walking the line of how can I add value to the community that I've built while staying compliant. But I think that I've been so excited to see you and the folks at Overlooked, especially, have just done an incredible job of bringing the community into your fundraising process and talking about how difficult it is. There was a great quote from Harry Stebbings' podcast about, he said, everyone talks about how hard fundraising is and says it's the hardest thing they've ever done. And then you actually start doing it and you're like, oh, wow, this is definitely the hardest thing that I've ever done. That's the one thing I wish I could have shared more of is it is a very difficult journey. But it's sometimes like you have to laugh at it. Like getting your first million dollar no is such a surreal, surreal experience.

[SPEAKER_01]
There's nothing positive about getting the no.

[SPEAKER_00]
It's just not yet.

[SPEAKER_01]
No, it's not. I mean, it's interesting for context. From June of 2020, September of 2020, I had over 1,100 meetings, right? And from like June 2020 to June of 2021, I had close to 4,000 meetings. So I just had a bunch of meetings, right? And so I never went into them thinking about money as I was about learning and making connections if the money happened, great. And so when people would pass, I'd be like, well, I never asked for it anyway, so thanks. It's cool. I don't have a GP commit, which, you know, other GPs can be mad at me about. I'm sorry. I just, I'm broke. Like, I mean, if you can't get over the fact that I don't have the money to be able to put in my own capital into this fund, and you think that's going to stop me from doing everything humanly possible? Like, the whole point of putting in a GP commit is just so that they can feel like you have skin in the game. So, like, they feel like you're going to be attached to this fund as they are. It's like, no, this is my career. Like, if this fund doesn't work, like, I'm out of work, essentially. You know, my track record's not as long, so I've had LPs passed for that, you know. I probably have had LPs passed because I'm big, black, and with dreadlocks. I don't know. I can only surmise, right? But I will say, you know, we all have these moments in fundraising. But as you go, you have these moments where, like, you get on the winning streak where, like, every meeting you have, you're closing and you're winning and you're feeling good. And you're like, oh, this fund's going to be closed in no time. And then all of a sudden you get a no that you weren't expecting or a string of no's. And it just kind of resets you. Like, I was used to that. But I will say, you know, I've had talks with other fund managers where, like, those moments come up and it's like, dang, I wasn't prepared for that. No. I got to reset myself and, like, take a day and get ready to get back up on the horse and go back at it.

[SPEAKER_00]
Oh, yeah. That, like, regulation of your – I refer to it as an emotional thermostat. But how you stay regulated during such an incredibly rollercoaster style of emotions. I'm curious how that has changed for you. I remember watching this video when we first started raising and someone committed to a $10,000 investment. And I took a video and I was crying in it because I was so happy.

[SPEAKER_01]
I don't know if I thought about it too much because, like, again, I should say, like, raising a fund as a fund manager is the most entrepreneurial thing we can do. Right. Mm-hmm. And having had two startups before, like, it just all looked really familiar. And then I realized, like, oh, yeah, I'm building a company from scratch again. I said I would never do this. This is awesome. And so it's just more the regulation of you enjoy the wins and you try not to beat yourself up for the losers. Right. But I will say, you know, there's been several times where I've gotten the call and people have committed and I've, like, gone run around in my backyard screaming and yelling, like, I can't believe it. We did this. You know, the first time somebody committed a dollar to my fund. The first time I got the $100,000 check. Shout out to Scott Telsky. The first time I got, you know, a $500,000 check, which turned into a million check. Shout out Insight Partners. All of those were seminal moments for me that let me know, like, oh, like, this is possible. But then, you know, when you get the nose or you get turned down or when you have a meeting, like, everything is going great and then there's some technicality that comes up later or there's some due diligence thing that you're like, yeah, I'm not doing this 20-page due diligence package. Y'all can keep your money kind of. Those things are deflating. But, you know, I've gone through that grind before. And so, you know, it's just, all right, you know, take an evening, watch a basketball game, watch a football game, have an old-fashioned, and go back to it tomorrow, right? Like, you just internalize and you've got to go. Go to Buffalo Wild Wings. Go to Buffalo Wild Wings with your friends and vent about it. And then, you know, you go back to it. So that's really, you know, everybody's got to find their own way to kind of de-stress and let that stuff go. And you just can't dwell on it.

[SPEAKER_00]
It's hard learning how to take things, like, less seriously while appreciating the privilege that you have for being in the position that you're in. I'm curious, you mentioned earlier that your fund structure is different. I would love if you could expand on that.

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah, so I should say my basic structure of my fund is fairly standard. It's more about the process that we put in place for fundraising. It was really abnormal. And what I recognized was all the things I liked about rolling funds were, like, technological. And all the things I hated were structural. And I was like, well, if I just use the standard structure, can I do everything else the same? The answer was pretty much yes, right? So, you know, 506C, public solicit, work with Carta as a back office. They had a partnership at the time with a company called Anduin Transactions, which turns your sub docs and LPA and any other legal docs into a guided web form, which is awesome because all I got to do is send people links and they can get access to my docs. And so you can go to rarebreed.vc and click a button to become an LP. Tell us you're accredited and you will just automatically get access to our sub docs. Like, you ain't got to talk to me. You ain't got to worry about the lawyer. Like, you just go straight there. And we do rolling closes every three weeks. So as LPs commit, we would send them to Carta and Batches. And every three weeks we would close on a group of LPs, which allowed us to get capital as we were going. We gave our LPs three options for capital. I got the idea for that from 500 Startups Fund 1, where they made all their LPs put 50% up front and 25% each year over the next two years, which is like rolling fund is like people subscribe for quarters. So we basically gave people the ability to subscribe for years. We could do 100% up front, 50% over two years, or 33% each year for three years, with the minimum being 10K per year. So if you wanted to make a 10K investment, you had to do it all up front. I haven't had a single LP yet. I have a concern about it, which also reminded me that like all the things they tell you that you're supposed to do in venture, like you don't have to follow any rules. Like there aren't really rules here, right? Like there are structures and processes that have worked in the past for others, and they've just shared it enough where that became the prevailing thought, but doesn't have to be the only one, right? And so like those are the kind of things that we did differently. But, you know, the back-end structure, you know, there's a management company, a GP, an LP, right? LPs don't want things that are too crazy, too out of the ordinary, right?

[SPEAKER_00]
Yeah, you don't want like half your pitch to be explaining like some weird aspect of your back-end.

[SPEAKER_01]
Yes, like that's not helpful. But also that's one of the reasons why I did some of those long-form posts that I did. So like I did a post about we're not doing a rolling fund, but this is what we're doing. And I know there were LPs who invested in our fund who read that first, right? And so now that gives them a framework of, oh, he's doing something different.

[SPEAKER_00]
Absolutely. I think the whole building in public when you're working through things, some of those things take so long to explain when you atomize the different structures on the back-end of venture and are putting them back together in a structure that works better for, you know, the modern, the next generation of fund managers, in my opinion, will choose to atomize the structures and use them like little Lego blocks and put them in all sorts of different formations. So you've talked to an incredible number of funds and GPs. I'm curious what firms you look up to as a brand that you've admired or taken a little Lego piece of.

[SPEAKER_01]
Well, I'm a huge fan of the folks at Hustle Fund. I think Hustle Fund is an amazing brand. It's an amazing team. They do a really good job of supporting entrepreneurs in a very tangible way. Like I've been able to see it with some of our co-investors up front. I love those folks. I'm a big, I mean, everybody's a fan of Andreessen and folks like that, the incumbents, the Sequoias, the First Rounds. They're all a little different, but, you know, to become a top tier fund like that, that's the goal. But when I think about my fund construction, my fund construction is probably closest in line to precursor, you know. And Charles Hustle was like one of the first to really double down on this idea of pre-seed. What is pre-seed? Basically doing like 20 investments a year, you know, this larger portfolio, not as many board seats, really being supportive and helpful for their founders, you know, I love the work that, you know, Charles has done over there. And then, you know, when I start thinking about the firm I'm going to build out over time, my real, the firms I truly look up to are NEA and Greenspring Associates. And that's really particular because, you know, being based in Baltimore, many people might not know this, but two of the founders of NEA are from Baltimore. And it's originally a Maryland-based firm. And Greenspring Associates, which is a Maryland-based firm, one of the founders is the son of one of the founders of NEA. Those are the folks that I, as I was breaking into the tech ecosystem, that I heard about and got to meet first, right? Those are the folks who have been my mentors, my advisors, folks I run into at bars and get to talk deals with. Greenspring Associates recently got acquired by Stepstone, which is an amazing deal. It's like a $750 million deal kind of thing. NEA is a top-tier fund up there with the Sequoias and the Andreessons of the world. To have folks from that ilk who support me and some who are LPs in the fund, it means the world. And so I'm going to build the next large multi-stage firm based out of Baltimore. When people look at me crazy when I say that, I'm like, well, we already had two. I'm just the next generation in that line. And then as I think about, you know, I've closed my fund one and I'm looking at my fund two, my fund two is going to have a lot more elements of like a Greenspring Associates, which, you know, hopefully there'll be a lot more to come on that in the near future.

[SPEAKER_00]
That's such an incredible vision. And I have no doubt that you are the right person to carry it out. I'm wishing you all a success in that. So in terms of your investment style, why do founders choose to work with you in your own words?

[SPEAKER_01]
Founders choose to work with me because I tell them up front that they should treat me like an employee. I'm not always going to be the biggest check, but I'm going to be a meaningful one. And whatever you need help with, like, yeah, we do the VC help of, you know, I can pick up the phone and call an operator or try to find a rock star employee. But like, you got my cell phone number. Call me, text me for anything. Right? Like, yo, Mac, I need help just figuring out payroll. Okay, let's figure out payroll. Me and my co-founder had a big fight last night. Okay, let's talk about it. Hey, I got, I had this meeting with this VC. What does this mean? What do they say to me? Well, let's sit down and have a conversation. Hey, I got an angel investor who's getting on my nerves. What do I do? Well, let's talk about it. Should I do React Native or should I build a native app? Well, you know, let's have a call. Like, talk like you can use me for anything. Right? And so I think that's why entrepreneurs work with me. And then someone want to work with me just because they see the Twitter thing and they think I'm really cool. So, like, I'll take that, too.

[SPEAKER_00]
I love that. I really admired that about you and Rare Breed that you're really willing to go to work and go to bat for the founders that you support. I would love to talk about some of your recent deals. I know one just got announced, Early Bird. Do you want to talk a little bit about how you found that deal and why you're excited about it?

[SPEAKER_01]
Early Bird is an amazing one. That just got announced today, which is awesome. Alongside, you know, 776 or Alexis Ohangan and then Gemini, the Winklevoss twins, which is kind of odd. Like, those are like some names. I don't know if I'm supposed to be, you know, in the same breath of it, but I'll take it.

[SPEAKER_00]
Right? Oh, you better say that with your chest, Matt.

[SPEAKER_01]
But Early Bird's amazing because here's one of the secrets to getting into some of these really cool deals is I build relationships not just with other GPs, but with a lot of young people just breaking into venture. I was looking for somebody to talk to or talk about ideas or how you work in this industry. And so that actually came from a woman who I met who's working at another firm as a senior associate. And when she saw the deal, she brought it to me. And I thought it was amazing. I've gotten so many deals that way from, you know, the associates that people always tell you you shouldn't spend time with or you shouldn't talk to. Like, no, if you find an associate at a firm who thinks what you're building is really cool, they will be your biggest advocate. Right? And even if their firm doesn't do it, it doesn't mean they can't get you to a firm that does. Yeah. And so I was looking for.

[SPEAKER_00]
Especially when they can't push through a deal they're really passionate about to a partner meeting. I think folks find particular joy in finding a partner that believes in it as much as they do.

[SPEAKER_01]
A hundred percent. And so that's how that deal came through. And I got to meet Jordan and Caleb and amazing team, amazing founders, amazing vision. It's a cool product because, you know, it allows you to make investments on behalf of the young people in your life. The children in your life. Well, I have nine godchildren. And whenever they have a birthday or a holiday, I buy them a gift and then I buy them stock in the company that makes that gift or that gift represents. Right? Now I can do it in early bird. This just made my life easier. Right? So, like, this is already something I do. And this is something that I advocate for other people to do. Now I got a company I'm behind in support. Make that happen. Like, that's a win-win for everybody. So, I'm really bullish on them.

[SPEAKER_00]
That's awesome. Can you talk about some of the traits and founders that particularly interest you?

[SPEAKER_01]
Every deal is its own individual thing. Right? My framework is I look for exceptional people. Right? But what makes you exceptional can be different for every person. Right? Like, David Pickrell from a company called Par. They help gig workers better manage all the different platforms they use, find more work, and figure out which route is making the most money. This dude was working at a venture firm but cared about this problem so much that he was doing, like, two to four hours every day of gig work himself. And then he, like, went to another state and hung out with a gig driver who was making, like, $30 or $40 an hour routinely and just rode around with him for a week to figure out how he did it. Like, it's going, like, all these, like, off-the-beaten-path, like, chat rooms and blogs just to talk to these drivers in this community. And he's like, you care about this way too much. You are the perfect person to solve this problem. Right? And that's amazing. But then, you know, on the flip side, you got a founder like Sierra for the company Rebundle making plant-based biodegradable braiding hair because she had such a bad experience putting synthetic hair in her head. She wanted to solve a problem for it. Like, the idea of using plants to create hair that's safer on your body and better for the environment, that's just crazy. Like, who thinks like that? That's awesome. Specifically in Rebundle, the reason I made that investment, because they do have some competitors, one was they were the first ones to launch in the U.S. with the product, but two, they had a really strong brand. The founder, Sierra, spent time building her brand as an influencer in the sustainability space and then was really thoughtful about all the branding she put together for her company. It was a combination of an amazing founder with a truly amazing vision, building something unique that was hitting on some macro trends, right? Of sustainability and wanting to have better products for people of color for their hair, while also having a strong brand that was really carrying the company. And so that was, you know, all those pieces come together, that makes it an interesting one. But then, you know, we got a founder like Femi from ScholarMe, which is being rebranded soon. You know, the reason I made the investment in him is because he's the one who famously used a Venmo hack to get his first 25,000 users. He was, what, 17 when he told me he did this? Like, I knew he was smarter than me and everybody else in the room. I was just like, yeah, just give him a check and we'll see what happens. And he goes on the YC, you know, he raised money from Paul Graham personally. He just raised some significant capital. He was getting ready to raise more, you know, have a company valued at over $100 million here soon. He's a 21-year black kid from Baltimore. Like, that's incredible, right? And all I needed to know was like.

[SPEAKER_00]
Yeah, I didn't know he was from Baltimore. I got introduced to him through Vern at Real Time and Marlon at Impulse. And they were like, yo, you have to meet Femi. He's awesome. And I was just so blown away by his presence is one where you just, like, whatever he needs to do, he's going to figure it out. Like, you got it. Whatever you need to learn, you're going to learn and be so excited by it.

[SPEAKER_01]
So when I worked for the state of Maryland, I wrote him his very first check.

[SPEAKER_00]
Really?

[SPEAKER_01]
40K to drop out of college.

[SPEAKER_00]
Wow. Wow. What a crazy journey. So you've just come off a very long period of fundraising. How are you thinking of using or differently structuring your time as we're entering the wilderness part of being fund managers?

[SPEAKER_01]
Here's the thing, right? Like, I want to take a break. I want to focus on some things. I want to do some planning. But honestly, we're in a really crazy market. Things are moving really fast. Things are moving really high. And when you have momentum, you can't stop. This is actually something Charles Heson told me. You know, he's like, you know, you don't stop. If you got the momentum, you keep going. So honestly, now that fund one's closed, we're actually spending Q4 working on the strategy and putting materials for fun too. I'm excited about the potential for a larger fund where I can really bring, you know, my team on. But I'm going right back to the fundraising. And, you know.

[SPEAKER_00]
It's such a crazy story. So for context for those listening, Mac and I both participated in Joel Asset in Capital's Emerging Fund Manager Program, which is awesome. I highly recommend. And he hosted a family office summit, which is the first time I met Mac in person. And, Mac, I would love for you to share this story because I feel like it's such a great encapsulation of your dedication to venture. Sure.

[SPEAKER_01]
It's crazy. Joel asked me to moderate a panel. Like, I said, sure. And so I'm going to catch a train up to New York. But I made it so that, like, I would get to New York and I have, like, a 45-minute buffer to get to the event. So I get on the train and the train's running 10 minutes late. So we lost 10 minutes there. So 45, now 35. Cool. I get there and I call an Uber, but they want me to walk to a corner. I don't know New York. So I walk to one street. It's the wrong corner. I got to get to the other end of the street. I'm trying to talk to the Uber driver who's not being helpful. And as soon as I get to the corner where he's at, he pulls off. I'm like, awesome. Let me get a Lyft driver. Got a Lyft driver. Picked me up. My 45 minutes is now down to 20. I should still be good. We got time to get there. The driver starts driving and every street he wants to go to is getting blocked off. Why? Because the UN is in town. So not only is there traffic and streets are blocked off, my driver didn't know how to get to where we need to get to. Now I'm just watching time click away, tick away, tick away. And so we get to the point where like I'm clearly late. And we're just like, standstill traffic. And so I just jumped out of the Lyft, paid the guy, and ran to where the event was being held. So I walk in in my nice dress clothes, which I hadn't worn all pandemic. And sweat pouring down, I open the door to the room. And as I open the door to the room, Joel looks at me. He's like, hey, Mac. Glad to see you here. Why don't you come up on stage and finish this? I'm just like, okay. Give me a moment to catch my breath. Let's go. So I was like 20 minutes late, but still had an amazing panel.

[SPEAKER_00]
I think it was so, so synchronous that you showed up as you got to the question where you were asking institutional LPs about the importance of investing in diverse fund managers, which was just such perfect timing. I think that was such a great way to get to finally meet each other in person. And like, as you think about building your team, I think this is like one of the things that I'm thinking about as we wrap up fund one is like, how do you scale this effort? So I'm curious, like how you're thinking about how you're selecting people to work at Rare Breed.

[SPEAKER_01]
I'm being really lazy about it. So like to date, I have two venture partners and three fellows, all the people I either knew before I started my fund or who like chased me down and like wouldn't leave me alone until I gave them work to do. And so like at this point, it's just like, well, this team. And then there's a few associates at other firms who I've worked really closely with who have sourced deals from me. Like when I get a chance, I'm going to poach you. I'll work with the team who believed in me when, you know, other people work. So we'll see how far that gets me.

[SPEAKER_00]
Yeah, that's really powerful. What have you learned over this past year? What have been the biggest things you've been reflecting on?

[SPEAKER_01]
One, that you can do venture differently. You don't have to follow anybody's path. Two, just do it. Like everybody, like when you want to do something that people think is crazy, you'll get a lot of naysayers. But just do it. Like just go do it. Like I didn't even know if I could raise a $10 million fund. Like if you told me I could raise a $10 million fund in less than 18 months, I told you you were crazy. But no, like I had the ability to do it because I know what I'm doing. Like this is what I do. I am a good investor. But it can be scary. Like if you're not at a big name firm and everybody already knows your name and people want to throw money at you, it's a really hard road and can be really scary. And honestly, we don't talk about this, but most people who go out to raise funds don't. Right? Most people don't hit their targets. But don't ever let anybody tell you that you can't. Right? Don't ever let anybody tell you that you're not good enough. You're self-included. I've also learned that don't let money stop you from doing things. Like if you don't have the money, just start doing it. Because if you go about it right, there will be people around to help you. You know, famously for me, you know, I'm currently a Kauffman fellow, which is amazing. Kauffman does a fellowship program. It's like the premier VC fellowship program. It's like the Harvard VC. Right? It's 80 grand for two years. And you got to pay that up front, which is astronomical and like insane. It's something I could never afford. But when I got accepted into the program, I wrote an email to a few of my LPs. And one of them, who's a mentor and advisor of mine, said, yeah, don't worry about it. I got this. He's like, you need this opportunity. You need to do this. Go do that. I couldn't thank him enough. And there are other people in my class who had similar situations who found other people and other organizations to support them through that. And like for the longest time, I wouldn't apply because I'm like, I can't afford it. But I have to say that now being in, it's one of the best things that's ever happened to me. It's one of the best group of people I've ever been able to work with. So I learned that along the way. And just the power of community. Like people are fundamentally good. People want to be helpful. People want to support.

[SPEAKER_00]
Absolutely. Yeah, I loved it. I just recently today saw a thread about a founder who you met with and ended up turning down. But they went on to talk about how helpful you were in helping them pitch. If you haven't raised money for a startup before or if you haven't raised like a significant amount of capital, it takes a long time to perfect the art of pitching. And I think as a venture capitalist, you're seeing all of these founders come out to market and pitch and seeing what elements work. And then also as a fund manager raising your own fund, you get intimately familiar with what works and what doesn't in fundraising. So I commend you for sharing that information and helping that founder with their pitch. I think this topic of abundance is really interesting. You and I share the optimistic view of the world and a strong belief in not letting money stop you. I went to a state school. I was very fortunate. I got a scholarship and worked my way through. But that 80K price tag on the Kauffman program. So putting some feelers out in the universe for things that want to happen, hopefully.

[SPEAKER_01]
Did you apply for Class 27?

[SPEAKER_00]
No, I haven't.

[SPEAKER_01]
You got to apply for Class 27. Paige, you got to apply. You got to apply. Now that we're here, I need you to apply to Kauffman.

[SPEAKER_00]
You're putting me on the spot.

[SPEAKER_01]
Yes. No questions asked, just apply. We'll figure everything else out.

[SPEAKER_00]
I want to hear more about your experience at the retreat because you posted a picture on Twitter at 1440 Multiversity, which is an incredible campus that was built by one of the founders of Jupiter Networks in hopes that folks would come to get more multidisciplinary education. And I went to a conference that really impacted the future of my life called Hive Global Leaders in 2019 there. So I'd love to hear more about your experience.

[SPEAKER_01]
Well, I'll say this, right? At Kauffman, they're all about helping you understand yourself so that you can be a better leader and a better person first and then a better investor second. They spend a lot of time helping you understand yourself, the way you think, the way you perceive, the way people perceive you. So help you better understand the world around you, how to work and operate the world around you, how to be a better conduit in the world. And then we dig into all the VC stuff. As a VC, everything we do is transactional. Most people look at it as checkbooks, right? When you're in Kauffman, you're around people who have the same understanding of the world and what we do, but allow you to be in a place where you can be truly open, transparent, and vulnerable, right? Where you can share the most personal of things and have a group of folks to rally around you who you can also do transactional things with. We were there, class 26 and class 25 at the same time and got to share notes, to spend time, to like fellowship together. And it was there that, again, somebody I truly respect and look up to talked to me and gave me some advice and gave me a push to think bigger and do bigger.

[SPEAKER_00]
I think that has been so instrumental in my journey as well. You shared that when you started, you would have never believed that you could have raised the amount of money that you did in the time that you did. And I sure as hell felt that way. And it was interesting. I don't know if you experienced this, but towards the end of our fundraise, people would be like, so why are you like only raising this amount of money? And I just would laugh and think back to the time where I was like, honestly, I thought this was impossible like six months ago. So I'm still trying to come to terms with it. And I think the power of meeting and having intimate conversations with folks who have done more is like the same as seeing someone run the four minute mile. It's like you didn't think it was possible. And then you see people do it and you do it yourself. I'm curious who in your journey has been instrumental in giving you those pushes. And what was the advice that they shared with you?

[SPEAKER_01]
Well, Charles Hudson has been really instrumental in somebody I can go to for things. Marla Nichols as well. Niv from Shrug Capital. Elizabeth Yen from Hustle Fund, who was one of the first GPs to commit money to my fund on our first call ever. And now she's like legitimately a good friend, which is crazy. Like I met her on Twitter and like now she's a friend. Vlad, who helped launch Foot Locker's corporate venture arm is now with Main Street Capital Partners. Vlad, you know, he's a black guy from New York who's a GP in a billion dollar fund. He's in my Kaufman class and he's one of the guys who pulled me aside and told me like, you know, you can do this. You know, he gave, he legitimately gave me a pep talk. And like eight o'clock at night walking around 1440. And I can never thank him enough for that. Right. But all the people I mentioned have been truly instrumental for me. And then also Vince Talbert, who was one of the co-founders of Build Me Later, a company that got acquired by PayPal for a billion dollars back in the day. You know, he's a, he's a Maryland guy. You know, he's been an advisor of mine since I was an entrepreneur. And, you know, to have him support and always have my back, it's been great. And there's been tons of other folks. So if I didn't say your name, sorry. Actually, you know what? I'm going to shout out one of my LPs, Zach Silverman. So Zach Silverman's incredible because he loves to tell the story that he literally had the ability to make an investment in one emerging fund manager. He made it in Rare Breed. And he did it through his parents because he wasn't considered accredited, but his parents are. And, you know, he got me to sit down with his parents and explain to everything. He made the investment. And I can't tell you how supportive that man has been. Like, he legitimately loves Rare Breed. Like, and granted, he's not our biggest check, but he truly believed in what we're building. Like, no matter how big our fund gets over time, he'll always have a spot. Right? No matter how big or small a check he wants to write, like, he will always be a member of the Rare Breed family. So I'm really happy to have him as Nelby.

[SPEAKER_00]
I love that. Well, Mac, our time today is coming to an end. But I always enjoy our conversations, and this is no exception. Before we part ways, do you have any advice for folks that are looking to get into venture?

[SPEAKER_01]
My advice is network is key. However you build your network. You know, I use Twitter. You can use LinkedIn. You can go to events, whatever. But this is a network industry. Be all the, try to reach out and meet all the folks you can. Reach out to me. Reach out to Paige. Reach out to emerging managers. Reach out to experience managers. You'll be surprised how many people will take that meeting with you. And when you do, be very thoughtful in learning as much as you can. And make sure you take down notes on what it is that they and their fund is interested in. Because not only should you be meeting fund managers, you should also be meeting companies. All right? That way, as you find companies that you think are incredible, that fit the thesis of some of the fund managers you're meeting, start making introductions. You know, start building a name for yourself as somebody who has strong deal flow. Because deal flow will get you hired. And if thought leadership is where you want to be, start writing. Whether it be a sub stack, tweets, LinkedIn, blog posts, I don't care. Start writing so people can understand your personal viewpoint on the world in some aspect of investing. Whether it be the metaverse, whether it be NFTs, whether it be crypto or fintech or consumer, whatever it is. Let people know that you have a point of view. That'll serve you well. Those are two tangible things I can put out there.

[SPEAKER_00]
I love that. Well, thank you so much for your time, Nick. I so appreciate it. I had so much fun today.

[SPEAKER_01]
Me too, Paige. Thanks for having me.

[SPEAKER_00]
Thanks so much for tuning in today to Seed to Harvest. If you enjoyed this episode, be sure to subscribe wherever your favorite podcast listening platform is. I'll be releasing new episodes weekly. And if you have any questions or comments, feel free to let me know on Twitter. That's Paige Finn, Paige, and then Finn with three Ns. Thanks, and see you again next week.

Leading fund managers have made over 10,000 investments into 6,000 startups via AngelList, all online and all in one place. And with the recently announced rolling funds, you can easily find and invest in these top managers on angellist.com forward slash rolling. But that is quite enough for me, so now I'm so excited to hand over to Mac the VC, founder and managing partner at Rare Breed VC. Three, two, one, zero. You have now arrived at your destination. Mac, this is such a joy to do. I've wanted to do this for a long time, having been a bit of a fan of your Twitter. So, huge pleasure. And thank you so much for joining me today.

[SPEAKER_01]
Thank you for having me here, man. This is like a crazy moment for me to actually be on the 20-minute VC show. Like, it's truly an honor.

[SPEAKER_00]
I mean, listen, it is great to have you here. But I want to start with a little bit of context, because, you know, you've heard the show many times that, oh, I serendipitously fell into venture from being at Harvard Business School and Google, and it was just so surprising to me. It's not your background. So, tell me, how did you make your way into venture, and what was that entry point for you?

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah, it's weird. Like, it's like, I was a software engineer, and I was a government contractor for years. I then went on to be a two-time founder. But my second company wasn't a success, it was a failure. And so, I had ended up working at a marketing firm for a year. That firm ended up getting a client I didn't agree with ethically. And so, I quit. But when I quit, I didn't have any plans. And so, I quit on a Friday. And the very next Monday, I get this email saying, the investment arm for the state of Maryland's hiring. I'm like, okay. I don't have a college degree. I don't have a finance background. But I know startups, and I know a lot of people in Baltimore. Let's go ahead and try this. Four and a half months later, they hired me. So, I broke in.

[SPEAKER_00]
I love that. Can I ask one thing? It's just like, you know, I've failed many times. You know, I failed to get jobs when I was early. I got rejected by many venture firms, which not many people know. But we're going to have an open conversation today. This is going to be a fun one. When you failed with the startup, how did you manage that? And how did you deal with that person? It's such a tough time.

[SPEAKER_01]
I didn't deal with it well, right? I basically got burnt out, told my investors, hey, thanks, but no thanks. Here's what little money we have left. You can all have it back. And I basically hid in my house for six months because I didn't want to see anybody or talk to anybody. And I was basically depressed. Because to fail in such a public way, when you got all these people and supporters around you, everybody's telling you how great you are, how smart you are, how you're going to be the next this, the next that. And then it doesn't work out. It felt terrible. Like, I spent all this time networking and being around people to, like, not wanting to see anybody. I didn't want to have to explain what happened. I didn't want to have anybody ask me, like, how's your startup doing? And maybe think about it. Did the smile. I'm like, ah, we're doing okay. And so I was just stuck in my house. Then something incredible happened. I recognized the people who truly cared about me and loved me didn't care. Whether or not I succeeded in that startup didn't change the way they thought about me or change how smart they thought I was or how much they respected me. Love and respect from your friends and your family members can truly be unconditional. And so when I looked up and everybody was like, eh, so what? Like, you've done all these other amazing things. You had one thing that didn't work out. Oh, boo-hoo. Like, it's okay. You have a great skill set. If you need to, you can always get a job. Are you coming over for the holiday dinner? And everybody's like, okay, so do something else. But let's go grab a drink, go to a bar and watch a game. Like, we miss you. And so that was really liberating.

[SPEAKER_01]
Welcome to another episode of Venture Unlocked, the podcast that takes you behind the scenes of the business of venture capital. I'm your host, Samir Khadji, and today's episode is a special one as we completely scrapped the normal interview format and had a fun water cooler discussion with two of the brightest and most transparent minds in the industry, Roy Bahad of Bloomberg Beta and Matt Conwell of Rare Breed Ventures. We had a great time talking about all of the challenges and opportunities that exist in venture today. Specifically in this episode, we discuss Rare Breed's unique 506C-driven public fundraise, the concept of seeding emerging managers, why GP commit as a percentage of a fund is outdated as a measure of GP alignment, and what they see as the immediate future of tech and venture. Now, without further ado, let's get into the episode to hear all of this and more. Mac and Roy, so great to have you guys on the show.

[SPEAKER_02]
Great to be here. Yeah, fun. I'm happy this came together. I love it when a Twitter plan comes together.

[SPEAKER_01]
I've been super pumped about this episode, both because I love talking about emerging manager and fund ones, but you guys are two of the most transparent people in the universe, really for the benefit of the ecosystem. And a lot of people know who you guys are, but I want to start with you, Mac. You launched Rare Breed, the fundraise recently. Tell us a little bit about the fund and the ethos.

[SPEAKER_00]
Yeah, so Rare Breed, we're raising a $10 million pre-seed to seed fund. Really, our sweet spot is anything sub $10 million post-money valuations. We are doing it under 506C, so I can publicly disclose and talk about it. So you can ask me anything and I can answer anything. At this point, we've soft-circled about half of the $10 million already. We're now starting to send out subscription docs and get people to put money into the fund. Talking about the ethos, I'm really looking to invest in companies primarily outside the major tech hubs, so outside of Silicon Valley, New York, and Massachusetts. We will invest in those areas opportunistically, but that's not where the bulk of the deal flow will come from. And looking to be the first or one of the first investors into every company we invest in, target check size $250,000, which is a little bit larger than what you typically see at pre-seed, meaning that we're going to have a slightly more concentrated portfolio. So looking to have somewhere in the neighborhood of 24 to maybe 30 companies in total. And because we invest so early, we are industry agnostic. We don't do life sciences because, like, not the skill set. I don't know how to evaluate it therapeutic. I don't do just about anything else. But even though we go really early, we do look for two key things, right? So if it's a software tech-enabled company, we like to see a clearly repeatable or unique customer acquisition strategy. And if it's a physical product, we typically like physical products in consumer markets that have lacked innovation over the last decade or so, 10 years or plus. Because those two founders tend to be out-of-the-box thinkers and out-of-the-box problem solvers. And that's what we define as a rare breed entrepreneur.

[SPEAKER_01]
Well, that's a great overview, Mac. And I do want to get into the fundraise. But what really struck me about your fundraise in particular is that you decided to go down the 506C path where most managers go down the traditional 506B. But you didn't go down the rolling fund route. Tell us a little bit about what led to that decision.

[SPEAKER_00]
A lot of this just has to coincide with the fact that when I started soft-circling money and thinking about raising a fund was around the same time I started to become more active on Twitter. So from June to now, I've gone from 2,500 followers to 19,000. And within that, I saw a lot of value out of the community I was building on Twitter. And so AngelLess came out with their rolling fund and how the GPs could publicly disclose about their fundraise. And I thought that was really interesting. And that would allow me to harness the power that I've created on Twitter. But then when you start to dive into it, the way rolling funds do their LP returns, it's kind of, it's a little weird. There's a lot of intricacies to it. And what bothered me was a lot of my earliest LPs or earliest supporters were people who've been supporters of mine for like the last 10 years. They've seen my journey from a software developer to an entrepreneur to now being an investor and now wanting to be LPs. I wanted to make sure that they got the upside of every company I invested in, not a fund one, not just based off the sum amount of quarters they invested in. And so I decided, you know, not to do the rolling fund. But then I took a step back and I looked at it and I was like, why are rolling funds so cool? Because you can publicly solicit. It almost feels like a crowdfunding because you can just go to a website and click a button to subscribe. And then you get access to capital very quickly, right? You don't have these traditional closers. You get your access to the first quarter of money right away. And when I looked at it, none of those had to do with the actual rolling part. They were all kind of just technological and front facing. But all the issues that I had with it were structural. So I said, OK, let's remove the structural part and just do the front facing part. And so I said, well, you can just do that on the traditional front. And so me and my team kind of came together like, how would we set this up? And so we said, OK, well, if we want to be able to publish these goals, all of this is 506E. OK, bam. The downside on that is every investor must be an accredited investor. I don't have the option of having up to 35 unaccredited investors. And that means that every LP that comes into the fund has to go through a KYC process. Well, most funds do that anyway. That really wasn't that much of a downside. So we can do that. Having a website to come up and give people access to our docs. At first, we thought we were going to have to figure out a way to code it so people filled out a form. And then we would take the inputs and dynamically fill out a PDF file that people could then digitally sign. But luckily, Carta, who we use for our back office, they have a partnership with a product called Anduin. And so what Anduin does is they take subscription docs specifically and turn them into a guided signature process where all the fields are dynamic. That fit that part perfectly. And then the last piece was how do we get access to the capital right away? And that one was a little tricky. And so when we talked to Carta, they basically said, you know, we can't do it. We could do it so that whenever an LP signs up to put money in the fund, we could send them money right away. But it'd be easier for us to manage it if we just did a close every Friday. And we said, cool, we'll do weekly closes. So every week as a pool of LPs come in, we close those LPs that Friday and we can get access to that money right away, which gives us a little bit more flexibility and gives us access to it. And the way we handle this, we draw the money down into an escrow and then we pull the money from the escrow as we make investment, right? So that's kind of the way we set it up.

[SPEAKER_01]
Thanks, Mac, for sharing that. There's a lot to unbundle there. And I know a lot of the listeners here are considering raising a fund either using the rolling fund structure or at the very least thinking about 506C as a provision to allow them to publicly solicit. And we'll get into that during the show. But turning to you, Roy, for a minute, tell us a little bit about how you work with Fund One managers specifically and maybe take us back to when you met Mac.

[SPEAKER_02]
So first of all, I just want to say, if there are people out there who are looking to invest in funds as a way of, A, getting great LP returns, and B, learning about the startup ecosystem, which is where a lot of Fund One LPs do, hard to imagine you could do much better than backing Mac. And I'll dissect why I think that in a second, and we can talk about our experiences. And I'll use my view on that to explain how I see the ecosystem. So, you know, I was a founder. I would meet with VCs all the time, you know, raising money, whatever. And I had this feeling of like, man, these guys, like some of the stuff they do, I just don't understand why they do it. So maybe I just don't get it. And some of it is like, hmm, maybe they suck at their jobs. And, you know, one example of that is a lot of them were very closed about information in ways that just seemed harmful to them. So, for example, like you'd beg to get a meeting with somebody, go get in your car and drive down the 280 or the 101 and go to Sand Hill Road, sit there. And in 30 seconds, you'd be like, oh, my gosh, this person took this meeting because they felt obligated. And we're a complete mismatch for the strategy of their fund. I was like, why didn't it just make it easy for me to look at a website and see that? And so when we started Bloomberg Beta, part of our idea was let's just try to do things the way that we as founders would wish they had been done. And, you know, a lot of funds then were saying, oh, like serve the founder as the customer. But like then you actually talk to them and the GP would be like, yeah, sorry, I can't talk. I'm in Bali. And it's like, OK, doesn't sound sounds like marketing to me. And we're like, what if we treated it as more than marketing? We were just religious about it. And transparency was a big part of that, because I think transparency, while it's very time consuming and takes effort and you expose risk. Like I remember before we published our first version of our website, which is, as you know, I think, you know, is what was once upon a time the internal operating manual for a fund. And it's just redirected to a GitHub repository. You know, we had people on our team being like, wait, hold on. We're going to disclose the average valuation. Like what? Like that could hurt us in negotiations. Then, you know, the risks were real risks. And so we went out to go do it. And I think what this reflects is a mentality that and this will zero into how we think about fund ones that, you know what? Starting a fund, it's actually no different than starting any other business on one level, which is you're starting a company that's competitive. It has a product. Its product is investments. You know, you can choose who you see as your customer. There are definitely some firms that choose to see the LP as their customer. However, we choose to see our LP as a supplier of capital and a business partner. And obviously, there are many groups internally at Bloomberg who we could talk to about technology trends. And we have, therefore, a client-like relationship with them. But our customer is founders. Like our primary customer is founders. And when you start thinking that way, you realize, okay, well, why are VC funds set up in the way they are? And a lot of it has to do with the regulatory history. Like why are VC funds so closed off? A lot of it is because private equity funds were very closed off. And so they just adopted the habit. And when we see fund ones, what we see is businesses that create a super normal return because fund ones tend to outperform. You probably know the data on that, Samir, much better than I do. And then it's like, well, okay, well, why aren't more people backing fund ones? And part of it is they're just not equipped to assess them because what do you have in a fund one? You're effectively, for almost all funds, you're backing somebody's taste. And it's like, okay, well, how well do I need to know somebody to back their taste? And, you know, Mac was describing some of these people he's had along the way with him in relationships, like longstanding working relationships. So, of course, those people are in a position to back his taste because they know him and they trust him and they have a feel for it. And, by the way, very parallel to the friends and family round for an early stage company where it's like, okay, you're betting on the founder. Well, who's best position to assess the founder? Not some professional founder assessor who's going to sit there and look into the person's eyes and be like, I just know. You know, I remember I think somebody affiliated with YC once said, like, I just meet a founder and I just know. Like, that sounds terrifying to me because I think what we know about human judgment is, A, that introduces lots of biases. And, you know, by the way, enter racism, sexism, like, you know, all kinds of biases. Come on, we can't possibly be that good at that. And so what we said for Bloomberg Beta is, wait a minute, maybe there's a chance for some super normal return here for us as an investor. If we said there are startups out there and those startups happen to have the business model of venture capital fund. But if we can invest in them in a way that makes sense for us, maybe we can produce super normal returns. So then, you know, we started like looking seriously at doing that. And we realized two things. One is investing in a fund is actually not the same as investing in a company in the sense that you're just investing in one product that they will have for a few years. That company, the firm, will exist like the distinction between a fund and a firm. That firm will exist for a very long time. And we, as long term backers and founders, we wrote a few LP checks. And then like two years later, like, OK, what about fund two? And I'm like, wait a minute. Hold on. Like, OK, I guess that's a little like a follow on financing. Sure. Maybe we'll do it. Fund three. It's like we don't have enough money to keep growing with you. And then the relationship does kind of not end, but it but you no longer have an active business relationship with them in quite the same way. And so we learned about this practice of seeding, which I'm sure many of your listeners know about. That is mostly something from the hedge fund world, which is confusingly. It's called seeding in our world where we also have seed investments where people invest in the firm. And an early LP might also invest in the GP or the management company. It's structured in different ways at different times. And the advantage of that is it creates long term alignment. We're like, oh, no, I want to make money when you make money over your whole journey, however long that lasts. And we can get into, you know, the pros and cons of it. And, you know, there's just lots of it's new adventure, relatively new. Although my understanding is that Sequoia was seeded in this way. There may be some other major firms that were seeded in this way. I don't want to name names because if I picked it up privately, it's not my information to share. And we wanted to explore doing that. And so that's how we think about fund ones is we're looking. We do them very rarely, maybe at the clip of like one or two a year. The single biggest issue we run into is and this is something that we talked Mac a bunch about is, OK, now we're investing in your firm. What determines the value of our investment? Well, returns are a big part of it, but actually AUM is the single factor that matters more than any other. And the people who seed hedge funds, when I started talking to them about why don't you do venture, they're like, oh, because the AUM doesn't rise fast enough.
