And what I see and what happened was in the time of COVID everybody was stuck in their houses and everybody was watching the news all day every day everybody was on their computer. And then George Floyd was killed. And after George Floyd was killed there was this upcry and uprising of we need to treat black people in America and black people around the globe and people of color better. And that led to how do we treat them better in all industries and in venture we saw a lot of venture firms talking about they wanted to support founders of color. We saw folks starting to put together initiatives to support GPs of diverse backgrounds. You know Alpaca VC who's an LP in Rare Reventures they put together an initiative like this to invest in five they ended up investing in six because they found so many incredible diverse GPs to back. And what I'm very acutely aware of is there's going to be an 18 to 24 month cycle where we're going to see an influx of funding to diverse founders and diverse GPs. But that 18 to 24 month influx is going to be fully evaluated 10 years from now. And so that means all these founders and GPs like myself who are getting the opportunity to show the world that we can return capital are going to have to show and prove. Otherwise 10 years from now when people point back to 2020 as a vintage year they're going to use this as a marker of like okay we did that how did it work. And so that means GPs in my position and founders of color where it's not fair that you're going to be the benchmark for this industry but that's the reality of it and that is a reality that is not lost. So that's kind of how I view it.

[SPEAKER_01]
It's a really interesting perspective and look I think there's a lot of tailwinds here. I agree with you Roy also that there could be some dark times. I've been through three cycles myself. So at the end of the day I am incredibly excited about the future of technology and technology investing. You know I really appreciate you guys both being on the show. This has been fun and informative. I knew it would be. And Mac really looking forward to chart the course with you on Rare Breed.

[SPEAKER_02]
Yeah and Samir I just want to say you and a few others have been cracking open this very closed church of investing in funds with steady work. That's real value to a lot of people including me and I hope many others in the ecosystem. So thank you keep doing it.

[SPEAKER_00]
Full disclosure I'm working with Samir so I'm looking forward to charting this course and having you on this journey. I would be remiss if I didn't say you know we are still currently raising our minimum check size to date is still 10k. So if you're interested in becoming an LP you can reach out directly to me Mac at rarebreed.vc. M-A-C at rarebreed.vc.

[SPEAKER_02]
I wish it weren't a conflict for me to invest personally Mac. Seriously.

[SPEAKER_00]
Or if you could go to rarebreed.vc and there's a button here that says click to become an LP. The minimum will be rising at some point so get in now before the minimum goes from 10k and it goes up. Just got to put that out there since I'm 506c I can do that.

[SPEAKER_01]
Thanks so much for listening to another episode of Venture Unlocked. We hope you really enjoyed this one. To learn more about Mac and Rare Breed Ventures or Roy at Bloomberg Beta be sure to go to Apple Podcasts or Spotify where you'll find detailed notes on the show. While you're there please leave us a rating and review. And hit the subscribe button in order to get each and every Venture Unlocked episode as soon as it's released.

[None]
Thank you. Bye. Bye. Bye. Bye. Bye.
documents.title: Mac Conwell of RareBreed Ventures & Roy Bahat of Bloomberg Beta on the state of Emerging VC - Venture Unlocked 020

metadata.media_extent: entire collected audio file; episode completeness not independently verified

context.quote: I'm from Baltimore. study computer science was a government contractor with the top-secret clearance supporting the Department of Defense here Did that for several years. 2010 started my first company.
context.claim: Conwell says he is from Baltimore, studied computer science, worked as a cleared Department of Defense contractor, and started his first company in 2010.

context.quote: four and a half years, two accelerators in the pivot later. We sold that IP to a division of a Fortune 100 company, which was really cool. I started another company after that, put a new team together. That company didn't work out, so I had a win and a loss.
context.claim: Conwell says his first startup's IP was sold to a Fortune 100 division and that a subsequent company failed.

context.quote: Yes, I was working for the Maryland Technology Development Corporation at TEDCO. I worked there for almost four years. Like it was like three years and 11 months.
context.claim: Conwell says he worked at the Maryland Technology Development Corporation, TEDCO, for approximately three years and eleven months.

context.quote: I started off doing seed investments, very traditional seed investments, $100,000 to $200,000 and just like anything tech. As long as you were in Maryland and you were a tech company. you could fit into our thesis
context.claim: Conwell says his initial TEDCO work involved $100,000–$200,000 seed investments in Maryland technology companies.

context.quote: I ended up leading the initiative to create a pre-seed fund for underestimated founders. It's the only state-backed pre-seed fund for estimated founders here in the States. And I ended up running that for two and a half years. And then I also did portfolio management for you.
context.claim: Conwell says he led the creation of, and ran for two and a half years, a state-backed pre-seed fund for underestimated founders, while also performing portfolio management.

context.quote: even for us a rare breed i have a few venture fellows and some friends of the fun who are all gen zers they're super young they get to see all the coolest stuff and one of the companies we invested in is a company called monad dating and it's a gen z dating app
context.claim: Conwell says Rare Breed invested in Monad Dating and involved Gen Z venture fellows and friends of the fund in sourcing and evaluation.

context.quote: Yeah, so the manifesto is these nine key points that... really are where our thesis comes from and from key learnings I had, having built and managed to fund specifically for underrepresented founders in the state of Maryland.
context.claim: Conwell says Rare Breed's nine-point manifesto and thesis draw on his experience managing a Maryland fund for underrepresented founders.

context.quote: One came from me being out in the community, talking to people, meeting people. The other one came from a network. And that shows how VCs should do it, where it's not just relying on your network. You should have multiple strategies on the way you source deals.
context.claim: Conwell advocates combining direct community engagement with network referrals instead of relying on a single deal-sourcing channel.

context.quote: We're at $7 million, so we got three more to go to get to a goal of 10. We're also raising on the 506C, everybody, so we can publicly solicit.
context.claim: Conwell says Rare Breed was at $7 million toward a $10 million fundraising goal and was raising under Rule 506(c).

context.quote: Every new fund thinks they have this amazing new... differentiated thesis until you start like getting out there and pitching is almost like being a founder You think you're so differentiated until you realize you're not.
context.claim: Conwell says emerging fund managers often discover during fundraising that their proposed thesis is less differentiated than expected.

context.quote: And three was to be a little flexible in our strategy. Like day one, when we were launching, this is the strategy we're going to do. You Yeah. And once you get into it, start deploying capital, the actual... ebbs and flows in the market. They force you to reconsider some things in your strategy
context.claim: Conwell says deployment experience and changing markets led the fund to maintain flexibility in its strategy.

context.quote: I want my legacy to be that we built a large multi-stage venture firm based here in Baltimore, Maryland that helped propel a new generation of entrepreneurs. and VCs and fund managers. that look and think differently than those who came before me.
context.claim: Conwell describes his long-term aim as building a large, Baltimore-based multistage venture firm that supports a new generation of entrepreneurs, VCs, and fund managers.

context.quote: We have some really cool beauty and hair companies that we're investing in.
context.claim: Conwell says his firm is investing in multiple beauty and hair companies, without naming them in this passage.

context.quote: I should have spent more time building my network. with other GPs and other VCs all across the globe. and having more conversations earlier. about what the process was and what it looked like. one to break in the venture and two to start a fund.
context.claim: Conwell says earlier network-building with global GPs and VCs would have helped him enter venture and start a fund sooner.

context.quote: If you want to invest, go to rarebreed.vc. There's a button you can click to become an LP. You must be an accredited investor.
context.claim: Conwell directs accredited investors to Rare Breed's website to inquire about becoming limited partners.

context.quote: I'm from Baltimore, Maryland. I wasn't born here, but I was raised here. I've been here pretty much all my life.
context.claim: Conwell says he was raised in Baltimore and had lived there for most of his life.

context.quote: Education-wise, I went to Morgan State University, a local HBCU.
context.claim: Conwell says he attended Morgan State University, an HBCU in Baltimore.

context.quote: And a year later, my junior year, I actually dropped out of school and got a full-time job working for Northrop Grumman.
context.claim: Conwell says he left college during his junior year for a full-time position at Northrop Grumman.

context.quote: So I want to introduce our guest this week on the show, on our podcast, McKeever Conwell. McKeever is a software developer and an entrepreneur out of Baltimore. He was part of the NUMI Accelerator and he was later named Entrepreneur in Residence.
context.claim: The host introduces Conwell as a Baltimore software developer and entrepreneur who participated in the NUMI Accelerator and was later named entrepreneur in residence.

context.quote: No, I was in the third cohort.
context.claim: Conwell says he participated in the third cohort of the NewME accelerator.

context.quote: The first thing we did was... So the name at the time was NoBadGift.com. Angela hated it. So we end up changing the name to Given To.
context.claim: Conwell says his startup was originally named NoBadGift.com and was renamed Given To.

context.quote: To this point, I've now gone through three accelerators. I've done a XRA Baltimore and a new made XRA for my first company. And for my second company, Electric Dream Adventures.
context.claim: Conwell reports participating in three accelerators: two for his first company and Electric Dream Adventures for his second company; the accelerator names are imperfectly transcribed.

context.quote: All right, so my first company, Given to started off as this. Registry site right so you can create a registry for any day or event you know the list of all the things you wanted And your friends and family to crowdfund the money towards the item.
context.claim: Conwell describes Given To as his first company and says it began as a crowdfunded gift-registry service.

context.quote: And we were running that company for about four, four and a half years. And we basically ended up selling off our technology to a Fortune 100 company.
context.claim: Conwell says his team operated the company for approximately four to four and a half years before selling its technology to a Fortune 100 company.

context.quote: Real quick, let me shout out my two co-founders from my first company. Oh. Sam Henry. and Michael Washington. And my co-founders for my second company, Redberry. Mark Campbell. Kendrick Williams and Brandon Williams.
context.claim: Conwell identifies Sam Henry and Michael Washington as co-founders of his first company and names Mark Campbell, Kendrick Williams, and Brandon Williams as co-founders of a second company transcribed here as Redberry.

context.quote: And so now you're at Tetco. as a deal team coordinator.
context.claim: The host reports that Conwell was serving as a deal team coordinator at the organization transcribed as Tetco at the time of the interview.

context.quote: So TECO stands for the Maryland Technology Development Corporation.
context.claim: Conwell identifies the organization transcribed as TECO as the Maryland Technology Development Corporation.

context.quote: It is the largest funder of early stage tech companies in the state of America. We do about 40 to 50 seed deals every year.
context.claim: Conwell describes his organization as a major funder of early-stage technology companies and reports that it completed roughly 40 to 50 seed deals annually; the geographic wording is imperfectly transcribed.

context.quote: We also have our seed investment fund. which is where I work. which has three funds, one's a general technology fund, a cybersecurity and a life sciences fund.
context.claim: Conwell said he worked in TEDCO’s seed investment fund, which covered general technology, cybersecurity, and life sciences.

context.quote: The one thing though is To get funding from Tyco, your principal place of business has to be the state of Maryland. Because first and foremost, while we do investing, we care about ROI. We are economic development corporation, which means We care about jobs. Our overarching goal is to create jobs as well as making good investments.
context.claim: Conwell described TEDCO funding as restricted to companies principally based in Maryland and serving both investment-return and job-creation goals.

context.quote: Now I'm just a member of the overall seed investment team where we all kind of work together. to go out and sort deals and manage the company interviewing. due to due diligence on the companies coming in.
context.claim: Conwell said his then-current role was on TEDCO’s seed investment team, participating in sourcing, interviews, and due diligence.

context.quote: I don't even have a college degree. And, you know, the only thing I have to my name is I help. I started two startups in the You know, I've gone through a bunch of accelerators and how work with one.
context.claim: Conwell said he had no college degree, had started two startups, and had experience with multiple accelerators.

context.quote: We basically created a program where we were going to take over the course of a year. 10. African-American led startups. and give them $40,000 as early as the idea stage, all the way up to the prototype stage.
context.claim: Conwell described a program intended to fund ten African-American-led startups with $40,000 each from idea through prototype stage over one year.

context.quote: And I manage him on that program.
context.claim: Conwell said he managed the minority-focused pre-seed program he described.

context.quote: And what I mean is, It used to be in the music industry, and this thing with venture capital in the tech world, where somebody would come out and be this amazing artist, right? You would hear somebody, they have this talented voice, a talented rapping. and This major company would bring them on. put all this money behind them, put this machine behind them, pump them up and put them out to the market. Wait. And it would take on a lot of risk to do that.
context.claim: Conwell used the historical music-industry model as an analogy for an earlier venture market in which capital providers assumed more initial risk.

context.quote: My second startup. Redberry, this is it was a concept around e-commerce platform. whatever, whatever, whatever, um, Instagram had a buy button on every product. I wanted to build a platform. I looked and felt like Instagram, but it was just nothing but products and every single product had a buy button.
context.claim: Conwell described Redberry as his second startup and as an Instagram-like ecommerce platform centered on purchasable products.

context.quote: I was able to sign up. over 180 different vendors. in less than two weeks.
context.claim: Conwell reported signing more than 180 vendors for his startup in under two weeks.

context.quote: I am lucky enough to be... Part of that program is one of the mentors so Any. I think I've got more work coming my way soon.
context.claim: Conwell said he was a mentor in the HBCU.VC-related virtual university program discussed in the interview.

context.quote: And really what's next for me is continuing to do my work I do at TEDCO. continue to you know Be supportive and be somebody out here who's doing what I can for the culture. and to really prove out and grow this minority business pre-seed program that I'm doing.
context.claim: Conwell said he planned to continue his TEDCO work and grow the minority business pre-seed program he was operating.

context.quote: I really do have this thesis. around I want to be a pipeline builder. And. to that end. You know, at Tedco, I'm trying to help increase the pipeline of start of minority led startups. to have the ability to raise. venture capital. But, you know, looking at HBCU.vc, I'm also trying to help create the pipeline of the next. set of the next generation. a minority venture capitalist.
context.claim: Conwell described a personal thesis of building pipelines both for minority-led startups seeking venture capital and for the next generation of minority venture capitalists.

context.quote: Yeah, that was me. I had a video blog. I ran for a little bit.
context.claim: Conwell confirmed that he had previously run a video blog about venture capital and startup entrepreneurship.

context.quote: So I'm a software engineer by trade. I went to school for computer science.
context.claim: Conwell says he is a software engineer by training and studied computer science.

context.quote: So I spent seven years as a government contractor after that. My last set was at Booz Allen Hamilton.
context.claim: Conwell says he spent seven years as a government contractor and that his last such position was at Booz Allen Hamilton.

context.quote: We went through two accelerators, one in Baltimore, one in San Francisco. had a pivot and then eventually sold that technology off to a division of a fortune 100 company
context.claim: Conwell says his first startup attended accelerators in Baltimore and San Francisco, pivoted, and ultimately sold its technology to a Fortune 100 company's division.

context.quote: After that, I started my second company, which was Redberry. put a team together, raised some money, got into an accelerator this time in Philadelphia, and my team fell apart.
context.claim: Conwell says he founded Redberry, raised money, entered a Philadelphia accelerator, and then experienced the team's collapse.

context.quote: When I got there, I was originally on the seed investment team, sourcing deals, doing due diligence as part of the investment committee.
context.claim: Conwell says his initial TEDCO responsibilities included deal sourcing, due diligence, and participation in the seed investment committee.

context.quote: in 2017 I actually started a pre-seeds fund. there at the organization specifically for black-led startups to help try to institutionalize the friends and family realm. doing $40,000 investments to kind of help companies get the seed.
context.claim: Conwell says he started a TEDCO pre-seed fund in 2017 for Black-led startups that made $40,000 investments intended to bridge the friends-and-family stage toward seed funding.

context.quote: And then in 2019, The state of Maryland added a million dollars to the annual budget to make it a long term frontier in state.
context.claim: Conwell says Maryland added $1 million to the program's annual budget in 2019 to establish it on a longer-term basis.

context.quote: Now, I'm starting my own pre-seed fund, Rare Breed VC.
context.claim: At the time of the interview, Conwell said he was starting the pre-seed fund Rare Breed VC.

context.quote: It also gets other investors to follow you. So the really cool thing about what's happening with me on Twitter is My network of VCs who I'm connected to now has grown like quadrupled over the last two months.
context.claim: Conwell says his public activity on Twitter had roughly quadrupled his connected VC network over the preceding two months.

context.quote: I continued that going and it's been a really successful tool for me. There is a lot of noise like the majority of people you meet won't have any chance to be investors in you. But what they will do is they're all most of the people I mean with our VCs or angel investors. So now I have a network of over 400 co investors.
context.claim: Conwell describes investor networking through Twitter as a successful fundraising and syndication tool that produced a network of more than 400 co-investors, while noting that most contacts were not prospective LPs.

context.quote: So now as we start to build out a market multi-stage firm going forward. We have the skill sets to fit it.
context.claim: Conwell described an intention to develop the firm into a multistage investor by combining his pre-seed and seed experience with a partner’s Series A experience.

context.quote: You know, I get deal flow for my network. So, you know, top schools, local schools. um schools that other VCs don't typically think about like every state has their big state school
context.claim: Conwell said his deal flow comes from his network, including prominent, local, and overlooked state schools.

context.quote: You want to make sure you have a partner that also has access to deals that you might not have access to. Right. So you want to make sure who's ever on your team, you're not all fishing in the same pond.
context.claim: Conwell described complementary deal access as an important consideration when selecting an investment partner.

context.quote: Going to the accelerators and like becoming a mentor and accelerator just means you get the first look at all the companies there Right. So you get to see them before their demo days.
context.claim: Conwell described accelerator mentorship as a way to see companies before public demo days.

context.quote: So it's at MacConwell. or if you look up Mac the VC. you'll find me, but Mac Conwell. That's, that's my name.
context.claim: In the transcript, the accepted speaker identifies himself as Mac Conwell and gives the social handle MacConwell and moniker “Mac the VC.”

context.quote: You get 20% of carried interest. that comes like 13 years later. Right. um and so then you got you're working off your two percent management fee. 2% management fee is $200,000 a year.
context.claim: Using a $10 million fund example, Conwell explained that 20% carry may arrive roughly 13 years later while a 2% annual management fee supplies $200,000 for current operations.

context.quote: But now, in cases, you can negotiate for some of those back office stuff to be paid for out of the fund.
context.claim: Conwell said fund documents may permit certain back-office costs to be paid from fund capital.

context.quote: And like understanding that's really like, and that's why you've realized a lot of people making these starting these micro funds are already independently wealthy and have the ability to sustain themselves for the first three four years
context.claim: Conwell said the economics of emerging micro-funds help explain why many managers are independently wealthy enough to sustain themselves during the first three or four years.

context.quote: My first check written into my phone came from one of my classmates. you know, a good portion of my first $2 million raise. It's coming from classmates from VC Unlocked.
context.claim: Conwell reported that a VC Unlocked classmate supplied the first check into his fund and that classmates accounted for a substantial portion of his first $2 million raised.

context.quote: I've been able to close on some LPs with like just over Zoom calls.
context.claim: Conwell reported closing some limited partners through Zoom-based fundraising during the pandemic conditions discussed in the interview.

context.quote: You know, several of the founders I backed didn't have networks. And so I was their network. I made the investment and I gave them a net.
context.claim: Conwell said he has backed founders who lacked networks and then served as their connection to a network.

context.quote: For those who don't know, I started my career as a software engineer. supporting the Department of Defense with a top secret clearance out of college.
context.claim: Conwell said he began his career as a software engineer supporting the US Department of Defense while holding a top-secret clearance.

context.quote: I actually dropped out of college to take a job in Northrop Grumman my junior year.
context.claim: Conwell said he left college during his junior year to work at Northrop Grumman.

context.quote: Ran that company for four and a half years. Two accelerators, a pivot, and eventually sell the IP to a Fortune 100 company.
context.claim: Conwell said his first company operated for four and a half years, attended two accelerators, pivoted, and ultimately sold its intellectual property to a Fortune 100 company.

context.quote: started another company after that that doesn't work out so i've had two companies one one win one loss
context.claim: Conwell said he subsequently started an unsuccessful second company and characterized his entrepreneurial record as one win and one loss.

context.quote: I'm a software engineer by trade. I was a government contractor. 2010 I started my first startup a tool my best friends.
context.claim: Conwell says he was trained as a software engineer, worked as a government contractor, and started his first startup in 2010.

context.quote: eventually sell the IP to a Fortune 100 company.
context.claim: Conwell says his first startup journey eventually resulted in the sale of its intellectual property to a Fortune 100 company.

context.quote: That's in October of 2016. I do see investments for the state of Maryland.
context.claim: Conwell says he entered venture investing for the state of Maryland in October 2016.

context.quote: less than six months on the job. I put out a proposal to start a pre-C fund. for underrepresented founders here in the state. which in 2019, got added to the annual budget for the state of Maryland and became the first and only state-backed. Pre-C Fund for Women and High Norities in the country.
context.claim: Conwell says he proposed a pre-seed fund for underrepresented Maryland founders and that it was added to the state's annual budget in 2019.

context.quote: 2020, I decided to start my own thing.
context.claim: Conwell says he decided to establish his own venture operation in 2020.

context.quote: from the middle of June 2020 to the middle of September 2020. I have 1,120 meetings. And from that, I saw circle my first 3 million. 80% of all my LPs and my fund came from interaction on Twitter.
context.claim: Conwell reports holding 1,120 meetings and soft-circling his first $3 million from mid-June through mid-September 2020, with 80% of his fund's LPs originating through Twitter interactions.

context.quote: We've only been. Deploying capital since January 2021. It's April of 2022. We have A portfolio of 35 companies.
context.claim: Conwell says that by April 2022 Rare Breed had built a 35-company portfolio after beginning capital deployment in January 2021.

context.quote: We're an investor in a company called Rares. We allow you to buy fractional ownership. and really exclusive sneakers
context.claim: Conwell identifies Rare Breed as an investor in Rares, a fractional-ownership platform for exclusive sneakers.

context.quote: We're also invested in a company called Good Milk that makes alternative milks.
context.claim: Conwell identifies Rare Breed as an investor in alternative-milk company Good Milk.

context.quote: We're also invested in a company called Rebundle, which makes... synthetic braiding hair out of plant fibers.
context.claim: Conwell identifies Rare Breed as an investor in Rebundle, which makes braiding hair from plant fibers.

context.quote: But I tell founders to treat me as an employee because out of sight, out of mind is a thing.
context.claim: Conwell says he asks portfolio founders to treat him like an employee so they will actively involve him when help is needed.

context.quote: Treat me like an employee. Because I can't guarantee you I'm always going to remember. What's going on? I'm not always going to pick up on everything that's happening. So let me know. The more you let me know, the more I can help.
context.claim: Conwell describes his portfolio-support approach as founder-initiated communication that enables him to provide more help.

context.quote: one of the easiest tricks in portfolio management. Random text message. randomly message one of the founders in your portfolio every so often though.
context.claim: Conwell says periodic unsolicited check-ins are part of his portfolio-management practice.

context.quote: I'll cash out them a hundred bucks and call it a founder care package, but Hey. take the day off early today and go get yourself a massage.
context.claim: Conwell says he has sent founders $100 care packages intended to encourage personal rest or wellness.

context.quote: You should be trying to meet with as many investors as you humanly possibly can. so that you can get on their radar. And so you can understand their investment thesis and what they're looking for. And then you want to meet as many founders as you can.
context.claim: Conwell advises aspiring venture investors to build relationships with investors, learn their theses, and meet many founders.

context.quote: if you start your own angel syndicate where you might not even have any. But if you can get a group of folks who do. who you are going to be funneling companies to. Well, for the companies that they back are invested in. that still acts as your personal track record because you did the sourcing.
context.claim: Conwell describes forming an angel syndicate and sourcing its investments as a way for an aspiring investor to establish a personal track record without supplying most of the capital.

context.quote: The market's changed. We announced that in January, and the market's changed a lot since January. So we'll see. The market's changed. Thank you. Fun 2 will be fun, though. We'll figure it out.
context.claim: Conwell says changed market conditions had made the previously announced size of Rare Breed's second fund uncertain.

context.quote: The second is the founder and managing partner for Baltimore based rare breed ventures, a pre-seed fund aimed at founders working outside of the most known and most cash rich tech hubs.
context.claim: The host introduces Conwell as founder and managing partner of Baltimore-based RareBreed Ventures and describes it as a pre-seed fund focused beyond major technology hubs.

context.quote: He attended an HBCU, majoring in computer science at Morgan state was a government contractor for multiple companies, including Northrop Grumman and Booz Allen Hamilton is a two-time founder with both a successful and a failed exit.
context.claim: The host reports that Conwell studied computer science at Morgan State, worked as a government contractor, and had previously founded two companies with one successful and one failed exit.

context.quote: And before starting his own fund spent four years at Tedco, the state of Maryland back investment firm, um, to support their seed stage investments.
context.claim: The host reports that Conwell spent four years supporting seed-stage investments at Maryland-backed TEDCO before starting his fund.

context.quote: The majority of that was raised off of Twitter. I have 194 investors in rare breed. Of those, 162 put in 50K or less.
context.claim: Conwell says RareBreed’s first fund had 194 investors, including 162 who committed $50,000 or less, with most fundraising originating through Twitter.

context.quote: right i told so i told people hey you can put in 25 000 into my fund and you can split that up over two years Well, you know, if you're like, again, in order to invest in the fund into my fund, you had to be an accredited investor.
context.claim: Conwell says he allowed eligible investors to commit $25,000 to his fund over two years.

context.quote: I matriculated at Morgan State University and I was supposed to be in class of 08.
context.claim: Conwell says he attended Morgan State University and had been expected to graduate with the class of 2008.

context.quote: She's the reason why I started my venture fund. Like, I didn't get into this to have a venture fund.
context.claim: Conwell says his inability to secure sufficient help for founder Shauna motivated him to start his own venture fund.

context.quote: I would send them a DM telling them a little bit about myself and asking them if they were willing to take a meeting.
context.claim: Conwell says he directly messaged new investor followers to request meetings while building his limited-partner network.

context.quote: I have 1,128 meetings in 90 days, the soft circle of the first.
context.claim: Conwell says he conducted 1,128 meetings in 90 days during RareBreed’s fundraising effort, although the final phrase is incomplete in the transcript.

context.quote: so I'm doing all this. I quit my job at the end of August. I'm doing this in earnest in September.
context.claim: Conwell says he quit his job at the end of August and began pursuing the fund in earnest in September; the surrounding dialogue identifies the year as 2020.

context.quote: Every Tuesday and Thursday, I sent out an email. telling the story of one of the companies I wanted to invest in.
context.claim: Conwell says he marketed the fund to prospective limited partners through twice-weekly emails describing companies he wanted to back.

context.quote: got to January 3rd of 2021. and 1.3 million hit the bank account. I was like, all right, it's go time. Even if I want to raise another dime, this rare breed is here.
